en: The *Buddha Speaks the Sutra on the Samādhi of the Lotus* in one fascicle,
translated by the Śramaṇa Zhìyán of Liangzhou during the Song dynasty.
The Buddha was staying at Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, together with his venerable disciples, the bhikṣus.

There were one thousand two hundred and fifty [monks], seventy-three thousand bodhisattvas, and an incalculable number of Śakras and Brahmās from the ten directions who had flown there; all were profoundly proficient in supernatural powers. Furthermore, there were devas and humans from as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, along with bodhisattvas—such as these, numbering as many as hundreds of billions of times the sands of the Ganges—all came to the assembly and sat before the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra, Subhūti, and all the other venerable bodhisattvas were filled with doubt and thought to themselves:
"For what cause and condition have these superior persons all come to this assembly?"
"What extraordinary and auspicious signs are there?
At that time, the disciples gave rise to doubts; they prostrated before the Buddha, knelt on their right knees, and wished to question him.

At that time, the Buddha emitted countless rays of light from his mouth—billions upon billions—which gradually expanded until they filled the void with brilliance, shining far across buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, while the earth shook once more.
Thereupon, when it was fully light, they no longer saw the physical marks of the Buddha’s body; the great assembly was struck with amazement and deliberated together:
“Where has the Buddha’s samādhi gone?”
Each of them reflected on this and immediately returned to their seats to enter samādhi in search of the Buddha’s whereabouts.
Before their seats was a bodhisattva named Huixiang (Wisdom-Aspect), who addressed them, saying:
“Excellent, excellent!”
While the worthy one was thus contemplating, he could not discern where he had gone.

After a short while, King Rājagṛha, along with his harem, crown prince, imperial daughters, and thirty-two thousand court ladies and consorts, all followed him together to the mountain; having arrived, they did not see the Buddha.
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva Anabhikāṅkṣin asked the king,
"From where do your followers come in such great numbers?
The king, named Pratibhānaprāpta, replied:
"I have come because I saw the Buddha's radiance.
The princess, named Li-xing (Virtuous Conduct), then asked the Bodhisattva,
"Where is the Buddha now?"
"To what place have you gone?
He replied,
"I previously sought the Buddha, but I am completely unaware of his whereabouts."
The woman replied, "You are the foremost among the Buddhas in supernatural powers; you ought to know the place.
The Bodhisattva answered:
"Sit for a moment.
After a brief interval, the earth shook.
From within the earth, he emerged and sat upon a great, naturally formed jewel lotus flower, leaving those seated above him in utter astonishment.
The princess Kṣemadattā arose, paid homage to the Buddha, and standing before him, spoke these verses to inquire of the Buddha:
"Having just seen a great radiance, I suspected that the Buddha had some extraordinary purpose;
therefore, I have come with this great assembly, wishing to ask about the doubt in my mind."
On the contrary, they no longer saw the Buddha; their minds were filled with great wonder and alarm.
"We pray that you will explain this in full, so that the great assembly may understand.
Each then gave rise to a samādhi and sought the marks of the Buddha’s body.
Having declared that they did not know the location, they each sat together and deliberated:
"What further samādhi should we arouse, desiring to fully realize the Buddha’s intent?
Then a woman came and questioned the assembly:
"Where is the Buddha now?
With pure conduct and a sincere heart, I truly wish to ask a question.
I pray that the World-Honored One will grant me an audience, so that my mind may resolve its doubts."
"For the sake of the assembled multitude, please explain in detail:
regarding that samādhi mentioned just now, what is its name and where is it located?
The Buddha spoke to the girl Li-xing:
“Your question is most profound; I shall explain it to you in detail.
The samādhi you just mentioned is called the Lotus of the Dharma.
It is like a tree in a great kingdom that bears a single flower which covers a trichiliocosm, and its fragrance perfumes as many buddha-fields as there are sands in the Ganges.”
If anyone hears its name or understands it, they will naturally and swiftly attain this samādhi;
if those suffering from various ailments hear of this samādhi, they shall be spontaneously cured at that very moment, and the myriad diseases of their faculties will be completely eliminated.
The woman Li-xing asked the Buddha,
“What is meant by the majestic power of the flower that it possesses such wisdom?
The Buddha said to the woman Li-xing:
"The flower is the color of a single tree; there is no one who beholds it but loves and delights in it.
That which enables one to obtain it is the Lotus Samādhi.
It is the color within the midst of birth and death, a great radiance that receives form."
If people do not know, hear, or believe in this samādhi, and do not practice it, they will not attain the wisdom appropriate for a bodhisattva.
They lose the very foundation of humanity and instead follow along with the flow of foam; in the end, they shall never see the light.
The woman Kṣemadattā again asked the Buddha:
"Now, desiring to attain this samādhi, what dharmas should one practice?
How many matters must one practice to attain it among human beings?"
"I pray that the Buddha’s vast compassion and grace may moisten all, widely opening the discourse on practice so that all who hear and understand may enter into samādhi.
The Buddha said,
"Excellent, excellent!"
There are two matters by which one brings many to liberation and attains the infinity of eternal deliverance. What are these two?
"First, one knows that the Dharma-body is like an illusion and like a transformation; second, one knows that lust, anger, and ignorance have no root and no form.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"The Dharma-body contains all things, Manifesting as transformations and illusions, appearing and disappearing."
Lust, anger, and delusion have no form; they appear like foam on water.
When one observes the body and its objects, they abide as formless as an extinguished flame.
Arising from the union of the separated, all such conceptualizations are empty.
The Buddha said to the girl Li-xing:
"Furthermore, there are four matters that distinguish one who practices the Samādhi of Following Conduct.
What are these four?"
First, practicing the precepts without the perception of form;
second, practicing generosity without a recipient;
third, never becoming weary without falling into distraction.
"Fourth is the practice of wisdom, being without folly.
These are the four.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"One who does not break the precepts and is without fault, who practices generosity yet does not enter into [mere] wisdom;
who is without weariness and free from delusion, who is neither foolish nor lacking in wisdom;
who does not speak of non-practice, and though possessing practice, does not claim to be heading toward it."
"Samādhi can be entered; it has no location, no center, and no periphery.
The Buddha said to the woman Li-xing:
"Furthermore, there are thirty-six matters that constitute what is perceived within samādhi."

What are the thirty-six matters? Not seeing birth, not seeing death; no decrease, no increase; no exiting, no entering; not being outside, not being inside; no dwelling, no stopping; no color of water, no color of fire, no color of wind, no color of earth; no pain, no itch, no thought, no perception; no birth, no death, no consciousness; no greed, no lust, no anger, no resentment, no delusion, no folly; no stinginess, no giving, no evil, no good; no mind, no intention, no mental formations; not giving rise to various superior phenomena, not extinguishing various superior phenomena—just like a single formless image.
"These are the thirty-six matters perceived within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
'One does not conceive of thought nor dwell on non-thought; one does not practice the desire for forms.'"
The Dharma of non-action is the purity of the Lotus; it is empty and still, devoid of self.
It does not abide within existence nor enter into [the realm of] becoming; it is extinguished without form or image.
One does not contemplate good or evil, for both are equally empty and spontaneous.
The Buddha told the daughter Li-xing,
"What is seen through the Lotus Samādhi is likewise like this.

When the Buddha spoke this Chapter on the Thirty-Six Matters, countless devas and humans, as well as the great assembly of the world— including the king’s attendants, both male and female, totaling four hundred million— were all inspired to resolve upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
The maiden Li-xing, along with thirty-two thousand ladies of the inner palace and consorts, attained the joy of the dharma that is unborn.
Standing there, the maiden saw that all the people had resolved their minds on the path to enlightenment; her heart was filled with great joy, and she rose to pay homage to the Buddha.
Having circumambulated the Buddha three times, he stood before the Buddha and spoke these verses:
“The World-Honored One is truly divine and wondrous; He expounds the knowledge of the three periods of time.
Having severed the defilements of worldly lust and anger, He transforms and enlightens those adrift on the flow of foam.”
All have reached the city of non-action, where joy and peace prevail;
thus, among gods and humans, the earth trembles and quakes.
Today, the great assembly has gathered—billions upon billions.
In the future and the past, as well as in the present, may they attain spontaneity.
May I obtain great and universal grace through the majestic spiritual power of the Lotus Sūtra,
so that all people throughout the three realms may attain this samādhi.
May I encounter you in this world, always performing the deeds of the Lotus Sūtra;
may the world be free from old age and death, joyful and without sorrow or affliction.
May the three sufferings be naturally eliminated, and may all be as in the state of samādhi.
By contemplating the consciousness of aspiration within emptiness, the marks and signs appear spontaneously.
Teaching those who are like foam upon a flowing stream, one attains the realization of universal compassion;
with radiant and majestic deportment, one becomes equal to the Tathāgata in person.
"Aggregated and born from foam, / Through the preliminary practice of samādhi,
/ One is enabled to dwell within space, / Attaining wisdom as supreme.
Having spoken this verse, the girl Li-xing (Śrīcaryā) thought to herself:
"If you now wish to instruct others, yet do not perceive the principles of the Dharma, for what purpose would you seek to enlighten them?
The Buddha, knowing the thought in the woman's mind, spoke to her:
"What Dharma do you intend to uphold, and whom do you wish to teach?"
"Where, then, does the Dharma abide?
And where do people dwell?
The woman Li addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Regarding what has been said— that there is no dharma, no teaching, and no person—
the Buddha said to the woman:
‘There are eight matters for the non-existence of dharmas, six matters for the removal of the non-existence of teachings, and seven matters for the dispersal of the non-existence of persons.’”
The woman asked the Buddha,
"What are the eight matters of practice, the six matters of elimination, and the seven matters of dispersal?
The Buddha said:

"First, right view without deviation; second, right hearing without listening for faults; third, right practice without crookedness; fourth, right speech without prolixity; fifth, right conduct without delusion; sixth, right mindfulness without discursive thought; seventh, right intention without movement; eighth, right reception without seeking."
These are the eight practices for the non-existence of dharmas. What are the six matters to be excluded from the non-instruction (avijñapti)?

First, not to conceive of the existence of visible forms, nor their non-existence; second, not to conceive of the existence of sounds, nor their non-existence; third, not to conceive of the existence of tastes, nor their non-existence; fourth, not to conceive of the existence of odors, nor their non-existence; fifth, not to conceive of the existence of tangibles, nor their non-existence; sixth, not to conceive of the existence of mental objects, nor their non-existence.
These are the six matters that are eliminated.
What are the seven matters of the non-existent person that are dispersed?

They are: the absence of the color of water, the absence of the color of wind, the absence of the color of fire, the absence of the color of earth, the absence of the color of mind, the absence of the color of consciousness, and the absence of the color of formations.
"These are the seven ways of distraction.
Since there is no one to be taught, you should understand it in this way.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses:
"If there are those who understand the *Dharmapada-sūtra* and the essential verses of the *Samādhi*,
they should mindfully apply diligent effort and attain correct understanding through clear realization.
Having perfected the seven, eight, and six [perfections], one calculates that fundamentally there are no forms or traces."
Not receiving what one personally desires, One casts off thoughts and abides in tranquil stillness.
The teaching of the Dharma is beyond verbal instruction; One does not perceive the existence of a life-span.
Humanity is fundamentally empty and quiescent; Do not fail to understand that it is like foam appearing to exist.
Without removing or severing desire, one enters and exits without a place of abiding;
without pain and without thought, there is neither birth nor death, nor extinction.
To have mindfulness is toil and suffering; thus one no longer clings to causes and conditions.
Manifesting the appearance of desire, yet having turned back from that love toward the dust of the world;
observing the presence of illness and pain, the mind is ever united with its original nature.
Seeing through wisdom that thoughts are not empty, one abides in profound stillness within the emptiness of the void.
When the Lotus Samādhi manifests, there is no emerging, no entering, and no abiding;
there is neither seeing nor non-seeing, for all is empty. This is how one swiftly attains Suchness (Tathatā).
One is then able to practice the Dharma of giving, offering up wisdom as one’s almsgiving.
"Thus has the wisdom and so forth been described; all Buddhas praise it.

When the woman heard this, she was filled with even greater joy and exultation. She rose and paid homage to the Buddha, then leaped into the air to a height of seven feet and sat once more upon a vajra-lotus flower.
At that time, a bhikṣu in the assembly thought to himself:
"Is this truly a real woman,
or is she an illusory person?"
He rose of his own accord, prostrated before the Buddha, knelt with palms joined, and spoke this verse to question the Buddha:
"Originally I was born into ignorance, And did not recognize the meaning of the wisdom of the Way."
I do not know whether this woman, Śrīmatī, is truly a man or a woman;
if she is indeed a fixed person, why ask further about her practice of the Dharma?
If she is truly a female body, why is the question so profound?
Since birth we have served the Buddha-dharma, yet never before have we seen such a person;
what you perceive is beyond the ordinary—how can your wisdom be thus?
From what direction did you originally come, that you were born into a royal family?
What dharmas did you practice in past lives? How many Buddhas have you encountered?
Your diligence and vigor are such as this; the Tathāgata shall answer what you ask.
You are fully endowed with the precepts and truly possess right practice; you are able to inquire just as it has been taught.
He is able to endure with a gentle mind, and can even speak of such practice with his mouth;
but what is his heart and mind truly like?
I truly wish to go and test him.
By abiding in how many dharmas can one go forth and meet [the truth] without giving rise to conceptual thought?
If you truly possess wisdom, I wish to receive the essential points from your understanding.
Examine the teachings you have proclaimed; chant them widely so they may enter both the monastic and the lay communities.
"What kind of extraordinary mind allows you alone to have attained this wisdom?
The Buddha then said to the bhikṣu,
"It is due to various causes and conditions."
He then spoke in verse, replying:
"The daughter Li-xing’s fundamental mind established the root of her consciousness;
having been in this world for a thousand years, she has constantly practiced samādhi."
The mind understands the essence of all forms; Tranquil, it is identical with dhyāna.
This is truly a woman’s body, Not manifested through the power of transformation.
Originally from the formless world, She has now come into this world.
Continuing further, one acts as in the original practice; having so acted, one establishes correctness.
Without a body, one manifests the teaching of the mind;
universally recollecting the compassionate deeds for all beings, one takes the emptiness of phenomena as the foundation, not giving rise to the marks of causes and conditions.
The bhikṣu himself does not understand; why then wonder at this female body?
Failing to see that there is no fundamental basis, he instead becomes bound by attachment.
Seeking to transcend form through meditative contemplation, he is instead further disturbed by form.
Far removed from suffering, one avoids the three poisons; yet once having entered the suffering of the three poisons, you do not understand your own body.
You claim for yourself eternal peace, yet all things are like illusions and transformations, entering and exiting without fixed form or abode.
"The four elements are originally empty space; naturally they receive form and attachment.
Through the habitual constraints of craving, one destroys the fundamental and gives rise to the desires of the derivative.
At that time, eighty-four thousand bhikṣus, upon hearing the meaning of this verse, attained understanding and immediately resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.
Countless devas and humans scattered flowers and famous incenses, all coming to make offerings to the Buddha.
At that time, Śāriputra thought to himself:
"This girl possesses such eloquence; why does she not leave her female form to become a man?"
The Buddha, knowing the thoughts in Śāriputra’s mind, said to Śāriputra:
“You yourself should question the woman.
Śāriputra then asked:
"O Śrīmatī! What you have said is not an ordinary matter; it is as if you were conversing face-to-face with the Tathāgata.
Why do you not leave the female form to become a male?"
The woman Kṣemadattā replied:
"Venerable Śāriputra!

The essence of the Way and its virtue is to see well through wisdom; it does not perceive the four colors—namely earth, water, fire, and wind—nor does it regard the conjunction of the five sense-faculties or the six sense-bases as decay."
Mind, intellect, and consciousness are like illusions and transformations; they enter and exit without form.
Because deluded thought is not exhausted, one confronts the three currents and further undergoes the cycle of floating and sinking.
What is there to prize?
"Although his outflows are exhausted and his fetters are untied, he still harbors perceptions of impurity; he regards the formless as evil and considers dwelling in suffering to be happiness.
Śāriputra asked:
"In practicing the Dharma of the Buddha, should there not be words of censure or disparagement?"
The woman asked:
"Venerable Śāriputra,
what constitutes slandering?"
He replied, "To say one is good and the other is evil constitutes slander.
The woman answered:
"I do not yet understand, I have not yet comprehended.
What the Great Man speaks does not regard the small as small or the great as great; regarding the good and the bad, there is no duality—they are equal and without distinction."
To slander the body is to slander that which is form;
to slander the mind is to slander that which is formless.
Since the four form-constituents are empty, being neither form nor created, who is there to receive such slander and defamation?
Śāriputra replied:
"What you have spoken is the practice of great bodhisattvas; you are not yet a bodhisattva—by what cause, then, do you speak of this matter?"
The woman replied,
"By what means does the Great Man establish himself?
He answered:
“Universally and equally he speaks.
What is meant by ‘universal’?
To instruct the people of the ten directions so that they may distance themselves from suffering and attain the Way—this is what is meant by ‘universal.’”
"What the worthy one has spoken is not about 'universality,' but only about the toil and suffering of birth and death.
The woman said to Śāriputra:

"That which is called 'universal' refers to not perceiving a person or a non-person, a teaching or a non-teaching, nor any thought of a phenomenon or a non-phenomenon; this is what is called 'universal.'"
"It is not for the sake of seeing the suffering of birth and death that he wishes to teach them so they may attain the Way; this is what is meant by 'universal.
Śāriputra lacked the eloquence to analyze and answer these words.
At that time, the woman spoke in verse, praising him:
"Human beings are disturbed by the three objects of sense, And immediately become attached to the six realms of decay.
Confronted by the five evils and the ten thieves, They fall into the three calamities and sink into destitution."
The twelve links continue in succession; the three realms of form, sound, and smell are bound by the four attachments.
Not understanding this is called perversion; one sits and receives the treasury of an empty village.
Without cause, one sinks into the three realms of lust; cast by one’s own net into the deep abyss.
Holding fast to their store, they fear duality and non-duality; They extinguish themselves only to undergo birth again.
Truly bound by emptiness, they constantly harbor impure thoughts;
Yet they call this "eternal peace," claiming it is the attainment of true spontaneity.
These types fill Jambudvīpa, numbering in the billions, hundreds of millions, and tens of thousands;
though their activities pervade the ten directions, they do not benefit any person.
There will be those who follow and practice [their ways], and all together they shall fall into the current of the ocean.
One may perform the practice of the Great Dharma, entering the ocean to strive against the roots of desire.
By draining the sea until it is utterly extinguished, one ensures that because it is level, there is no returning current;
returning to the source and exhausting the chamber of desire, one causes people to go back to their native land.
His native land is named Wuwei (Non-action), and his title is Qingjing Tang (Hall of Purity).
Abounding in joy and purple-golden light, he enters and exits radiating brilliance.
Throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there are no Buddhas who do not praise and extol him.
Because the Dharma is empty and free from conceptual proliferation, it is signless and beyond the reach of volition or consciousness.
Like the vast flow of rivers merging into the ocean, even these cannot be fully described.
With a broad mind, he transforms and enlightens others, remaining naturally and eternally at peace.
"Reflecting only upon these worthy ones, I see that they themselves do not understand;
for no reason they have bound themselves, receiving retribution for what is but a phantom illusion.
At that time, the forty-two thousand arhats were all established in the seventh stage with correct mindfulness.
Eighty-five thousand Śakras and Brahmās all attained the birth that is non-action.
Sixty-four thousand noble women arose and paid homage to the Buddha; standing before the Buddha, they spoke these verses:
“Today, the woman of skillful conduct Has preached for our sake and for the multitude.”
Hearing the Buddha’s profound Dharma, my mind has been opened and liberated.
Truly desiring to know the Way and its Virtue, from where do they all arise?
When all things are gathered together, what divine and wondrous qualities do they possess?
Thus, together with the great assembly, there was none whose heart was not struck with amazement;
they bowed their wills and joyfully followed, acting in accordance with the teachings.
They desired to seek the World-Honored One, who out of compassion rouses and purifies the multitudes.
With a sincere heart they received Great Wisdom, as the Tathāgata manifested his divine transformations.
At that moment, their female bodies were transformed; with inverted aspirations, they sought to leave behind form and desire, wishing to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha, knowing my inner feelings, [granted their request].
Having fully awakened to all truths, they cause their bodies to become like those of Bodhisattvas;
proclaiming the divine teachings of the Buddha, they shall in turn transform others.
All the worthy ones, the great assembly, and the women rose together before the Buddha.
Bowing my head and prostrating, I pray that I may become like the Buddha’s image.
The Buddha said to the women:
“What you have spoken is truly from the depths of your hearts.”
"Now, as you wish to seek your aspiration, you must first repay your parents; next, it shall depend upon the King; only when you have received his permission may you depart.
Thereupon, the women spoke in verse, responding and saying:
"If one wishes to become a śramaṇa, One must first repay one's parents."
Next, one must furthermore rely upon a king to obtain permission to practice the Way.
It is not too late to seek the Way; one should simply be diligent and open the mind, understanding the root of the mental faculty, and regarding all things with equanimity.
Thereupon, he resolved his great purpose; his mind attained liberation up to the Way.
The Way arises from the liberated mind, remaining no longer bound by attachments.
Through transformation he mastered the observation of all views, as if they were produced anew from the mind.
From the beginning, know that the source is empty; know that all things are impermanent and suffering.
When the mind is distracted, it follows the current; whatever is perceived will have its counterpart.
Only when one no longer gives rise to notions of good or evil does one become a śramaṇa.
The virtuous women rose and went to where their parents were; kneeling on their right knees, they addressed their parents and the Great King, saying:
"Today, having received the king’s grace and virtue, we have come to the dwelling place of the Buddha."

For the sake of the noble daughter Li-xing, who questioned the Buddha regarding the profound and wondrous Dharma, desiring to seek the path of the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) for herself and all beings, the Buddha explained to her the beginning and end, birth and death, and suffering;
he taught that she was merely attached to form and desire, and did not know the root of virtue.
Since conditioned phenomena are impermanent and subject to the arrival of the three types of suffering, one must apply oneself diligently.
I wish to become a śramaṇa; I pray that my parents will grant me permission to become a śramaṇa, so that I may attain the Way and return to deliver my parents.
The parents said to their daughters,
"Seeking the path of spontaneity, each of you may see what is appropriate for yourselves and practice according to your inclinations.
Since you all wish to depart, I shall follow you."
"You should speak these words to the King yourself; once you have obtained his permission, you may depart. Why must you ask me?
The women prostrated themselves before the Great King and, shedding tears, said:

"A person within the three realms of existence dwells amidst the desire for form and perception, unable to attain self-mastery. Impermanence arrives suddenly, and there is no one who can take its place."
"I truly wish to become a śramaṇa together with all these women; once we have attained the Way through non-action, we shall return to deliver our parents. O King, please grant us our original wish."
The King said to the women, including Śrīmatī:
"I have long desired for you to depart and follow [the path] as śramaṇas; however, because your three matters were not yet complete, I did not send you."

First, they have not yet exhausted their study of all rites and teachings; second, they constantly delight in that which has not yet seen suffering; third, they indulge in flavors with their mouths, never knowing satiety.
For this reason, I did not wish to send you away.
If you have a sincere intention, then go without hesitation;
I, too, wish to become a śramaṇa.
The king immediately rose and went to where the Buddha was; having paid homage, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Having heard the discourse on wisdom, my heart is filled with profound aspiration and joy.
I entrust the kingdom to the crown prince and shall personally take refuge in the Triple Gem, serving at your side while receiving your Dharma teachings.”
"I wish to become a śramaṇa and seek the Way as the Buddha does.
Thereupon, the Buddha emitted light of various colors, its brilliance illuminating the ten directions, and the earth shook in six ways.
The devas played music that filled the void of space, scattering flowers and famous jewels that covered the trichiliocosm.
The mounds and hollows of the world became level, great mountains were transformed into gold, and withered trees grew anew.
Among them were those who were not physically perfect, yet all had their wishes fulfilled.
The withered trees all sprouted branches and leaves; naturally stirred by the wind, they all sang praises of the Buddha’s merits.

The flowers that bloomed fell of their own accord, and their respective fragrances reached the Buddha’s dwelling, where they remained suspended in mid-air, each reciting verses to extol the Buddha’s merits:
"Now, by the power of the Sage’s spiritual might, I have been rescued from death and restored to life;
my radiance and complexion have returned to their natural state, and I shall once again truly nourish the Way and achieve its fulfillment.
The lustful and chaotic colors of birth and death are like the season of withered wood."
Encountering the Buddha’s teaching on sounds, they return to merge with their original source.
The six colors sink into stillness; the four colors unite with the five desires.
Discerning that all phenomena are empty, one understands the Way and accomplishes the practice of the Dharma.
"To attain true meditative wisdom, To obtain happiness and peace,
And for all to rejoice— I bow my head in homage at the Buddha’s feet.
At that time, the various ones possessing the six supernormal powers and the arhats saw that the flowers spoke these words.
The girl Li-xing immediately transformed herself into a man and further became a bodhisattva.
As this one woman underwent these two miraculous transformations, there was no one among those seated who did not rejoice.

At that time, there were no women in that single buddha-field. Among the hundred thousand five thousand practitioners of the six supernormal powers, thirty thousand srotāpannas all attained the stage of avaivartika;
eighty-six thousand persons and anāgāmins all attained the patient acceptance of the compliant Dharma (anulomikī-dharmakṣānti).
Incalculable numbers of arhats further resolved their minds toward supreme, perfect enlightenment, and those who practiced the path of pratyekabuddhas were like Maitreya and his peers.
The King then entrusted the kingdom to the Crown Prince.
The Crown Prince’s name was Pien-chi (Vidyākūṭa); he prostrated himself before the Great King and said:

“Does Your Majesty wish to bestow upon your descendants the calamities of this physical body, or the merit thereof? If you bestow the calamities upon your descendants, they will suffer; if you bestow the merit upon your descendants, they will receive blessings.”
One should pass on to one’s descendants the benefit of the wealth of the Dharma, rather than the great sin of enmity that must be eradicated.

When the governance of a great state has declined and been lost for generations, and the people’s faculties remain ignorant of Great Wisdom—the path that extinguishes all evil—how can one entrust this to one’s descendants? How should one act?
"The King, my father, has issued a command that I must obey.
He immediately prostrated himself, took his leave of the king, and departed.
Returning to the palace of his own kingdom, he took charge of the realm and issued a proclamation to all:
"If one does not go to the Buddha’s presence to seek the unconditioned Way and practice virtuous filiality, one's transgressions will be equal to those of the three heinous crimes.
In the palace hall, the Prince applied himself with diligence, courage, and wisdom, extensively opening the mind toward the Great Way.
His mind was far more immeasurable than before; he immediately extinguished the evils of an entire city, and the earth shook in six ways.
At that time, the people all said:
"May the Prince attain Buddhahood soon; we, the great multitude, shall all follow him as his disciples and likewise become Buddhas."
The Buddha then smiled, and light of five colors issued forth, illuminating the buddha-fields of the ten directions.
All the people made this vow:
"May we attain the Way as the Buddha has; may food and drink appear naturally before us throughout the world, just as it does in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven."
"The bodhisattvas in that land are all like those in the land of Amitābha.

Having attained merit while staying in the palace for seven days, Prince Debatse (Dharmasaṃcaya) went forth to the place where the Buddha was, accompanied by a vast multitude of ministers and countless people, both great and small.
Arriving at the Buddha’s dwelling, he prostrated in worship and stood before the Buddha, reciting hundreds of billions of verses in praise, saying:
“The Buddha has attained the resolve of samādhi; His merit is most sublime and lofty.
The radiance of his marks and majestic spiritual power shine forth, Moving and stirring the three thousandfold world-system.”
Bestowing supreme wisdom upon others, his virtue universally enters the hearts of the multitude;
he moves and awakens the ignorant, so that none fail to receive the fulfillment of blessings.
He recites and chants the matters of the Lotus Sūtra, transforming the world and cleansing the various heterodoxies.
Those who were fierce and stubborn were subdued, and through harmony they further received gentleness.
Equally seeking the light of the site of enlightenment, worldly people receive their karma for a long time;
having departed from old age to reach emptiness and stillness, they do not die, yet they are born again.
Removing illness and distancing oneself from defilement and disgrace, the perceptions of form subside and toil is extinguished;
the hindrances are thereby eliminated, becoming pure and free from the dust of desire.
Contemplating the meditative absorption on desire, one spreads this practice and returns to the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Emptiness is eternally tranquil; it does not abide in non-abiding practice.
Without practicing, there is no cognition of dharmas; it manifests the accomplishment of radiant signs.
The fundamental dharma neither increases nor decreases; it is eternally settled in the emptiness of emptiness.
The Tathāgata manifests spiritual transformations, so that all may attain the true Way.
Ignorance becomes stilled in meditative concentration, and the mind is identical with non-arising.
I now listen to the preaching of the Dharma, as he brings forth the wisdom of the Lotus Sūtra.
With a mind of understanding, one may make vows, and all shall become like the Buddha.
Now, desiring to purify the city and the land, I pray that you preach the Lotus Sutra;
by what dharma-practice can this be attained?
How many matters must be understood to swiftly attain this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*? By explaining its wisdom according to its meaning,
may all be made to discern and know it, so that every mind attains liberation.
Thoroughly understanding the affairs of all phenomena, one shall attain them from within and without.
Whether this attainment is far or near, one may immediately establish Buddhahood;
yet how many more kalpas must pass, and from how many Buddhas must one receive [the teaching] over time?
"Wisdom and insight possess an essential core; in an instant they transform and manifest.
I pray that you will explain them in full detail, so that the entire assembly may come to know them.
The Prince and the multitude paid their respects and returned to their seats.
The Buddha said to the daughter Li-xing:

"If you wish to know the manifestation of the opening and elucidation of the Lotus Sūtra, all Buddhas of the future, past, and present have attained the Way and realized the Truth through this 'Parable of the Dispersed Body' chapter."

At that time, there were hundreds of thousands of millions of devas and Brahmās, incalculable numbers of people, and four hundred and eighty thousand bodhisattvas who attained the state of non-arising;
as for those who were śrāvakas, they all resolved their minds anew.
At that time, the Bodhisattva No-Thought addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Today the great assembly has heard the explanation of the essential matters of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, yet none have received its secret instructions."
The Buddha told the bodhisattvas:
"Those who today have expounded the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi* have all been granted the secret instructions.
There are kalpas to come, and each shall have their own land and dwelling place; for this reason, I do not speak of them further."
"If you do not understand, go there yourself and ask them all.
Then the Prince and the girl Li-xing (Liṅgī) immediately informed the Bodhisattva of what they wished to ask in their hearts; he then spoke a verse in response to each of them, saying:
"O Wise and Noble One of supreme wisdom, Why do you not understand the essential point?"
Those who harbor thoughts of seeking reward, All lack the wisdom of non-attachment.
If one speaks of specific locations, It is not the matter of the Lotus Sūtra;
One must certainly speak with the mouth, Desiring to hear the true, sublime voice.
Not understanding its beginning or end, they do not comprehend even what is said;
when shown the path of the Dharma, they are like those who are blind.
Even the great roar of a lion is reduced to a mere whisper.
Having received the secret instructions, one attains Buddhahood; yet one does not know how to pay homage to the Right Path.
Having received the instructions, there are lands and realms; these are likewise like illusions and transformations.
When there is an object of perception, a response arises; one no longer engages in prior conceptualization.
Observing the teachings attached to him, he extends throughout the past, future, and present;
with supernormal powers, there is nothing he does not know, yet he has no need for verbal expression.
Having received the secret instructions within emptiness and non-existence, he dwells in tranquil, effortless non-action.
Constantly settled and unmoving, it is unknown to those of narrow mind.
Expounding that which has not yet occurred, tranquil and without purposeful action—
this is the land of delight, where purity serves as the realization of the truth.
Not to dwell on the existence of thoughts—this is the peace of the blissful Dharma;
To manifest the marks and signs with radiance—this is the appearance of diligent exertion;
To have disciples and followers—this is entering the turbidity of desire.
"Without suffering or exertion, mindfulness remains; all is exhausted, neither arising nor ceasing.
Thus he spoke eighteen trillion verses in response.
The Bodhisattva was immediately filled with joy and spoke these verses in praise:
"I myself was born of delusion, failing to understand the words of the Superior One;
not knowing their meaning or the Dharma, I instead called them 'those who have not received the prediction.
The verses now spoken are exceedingly profound and difficult to fully express."
"I pray that you will manifest your original intent and engage in a discussion with the spirits.
At that time, the Prince addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Now these worthies still do not understand the essential; please use skillful means to open their understanding."
The Buddha then smiled, and five-colored light issued forth from his heart and mouth, illuminating the ten directions.
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; this smile must surely have a specific meaning."
"I wish to hear its explanation.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see this great assembly?"
Ānanda replied, “I see them.

“Now you have answered all that the Tathāgata has asked. Each of you is teaching and transforming beings throughout the ten directions—devas and humans as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—and causing them all to become Buddhas.”
At that time, fragrant flowers and the seven treasures rained down spontaneously, covering the trichiliocosm so completely that there was not a single empty space remaining.
The Buddha said to the prince:
"Such is the matter concerning the human body as explained in this *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*."

At that time, incalculable hundreds of thousands of myriads of people, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, all resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path, attaining the mind of non-arising;
and countless thousands of śrāvakas all attained the stage of avaivartika.
Ānanda knelt with his right knee on the ground and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be practiced and upheld?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
“Its title is ‘The Essential Collection of the Sūtra on Resolving the Scattered Emotions of the Human Body as Asked by the Girl Li-xing,’ [also known as] the ‘Dharmapada-samādhi.’”
If there are men or women who copy, recite, or read [this], it surpasses practicing the perfection of giving for eighty kalpas;
if they make offerings by prostrating before it, it surpasses a bodhisattva practicing loving-kindness for three hundred billion koṭis of kalpas;
if they understand it thoroughly and teach it to one another in turn, it surpasses making offerings to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
If there is one who hears this sutra even once, they shall no longer undergo the toil and suffering of birth and death.
As for those who do not believe and slander it, such persons follow along with the superficial currents and have not yet returned to the source.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"I entrust to you the matters of the *Dharmapada-samādhi*; even in a thousand kalpas, one could not exhaust them.

I have spoken only the essential truths in brief; receive, transcribe, uphold, and practice them, without omitting a single word, ensuring that the characters and phrases are correctly written and properly aligned."

The great assembly that followed the Prince was enlightened and liberated; each attained the wisdom of the Path and became like the leaders [of the assembly]. They rose, paid homage to the Buddha, and departed.
*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra*
